answer.evidence: The tile is a full-width 48px opaque block of speckled sand in two flat bands. Rows 0-15 are a darker band. A bright 1-row highlight at row 16 separates it from a lighter band in rows 17-29. Rows 30-31 hold a thin darker line and a highlight line. Both bands are flat textured surfaces seen from above. No band is a vertical face of 3 or more rows with its own shading, so there is no readable south-facing front face and no step riser. The step is suggested only by the lip highlight line and the lightness change.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a sand stair read as a few broad horizontal tread/riser bands, with light edge lines and a dark tan line under each step. Its 6 visible tones per tile are in line with the paving reference (7) and above the grass (3), and its dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outlines lean brown/tan rather than black. The weakness is texture. 21% of its 5x5 blocks are flat, against 0% in both references, and the bands are wide, mostly unvaried tan areas with only a few grain dots. The references show grain, speckle or per-stone shading across the whole surface. It has only 7 raw colours in total, so each sand band is close to a single tone, and the stair reads as stripes rather than a worked surface. Next to the references it looks flatter and thinner than a careful artist would accept, so with doubt it fails.

answer.evidence: The tile is 48 px wide and 32 rows tall, and every row has the same width. Rows 0-15 are a darker flat band (L about 180) and read as a vertical riser or cliff face. Row 16 is a bright lip line (#fff9b4). Below it, rows 17-29 are lighter (L about 205) and read as a horizontal tread. Rows 28-30 are slightly darker, and row 30 is a darker edge line, with another highlight on row 31 starting the next step. This gives a tread of about 14 rows with a front-edge line, plus a riser face of 13 rows. The structure reads as a stepped, three-quarter terrain tile rather than a flat slab, though the distinction between riser and tread is subtle.

styleAnswer.evidence: The measured facts are acceptable: 6 visible tones per tile against 3 for grass and 7 for paving, and 0% neutral dark edge pixels, so the edges lean brown rather than black. But 21% near-flat coverage against 0% in both references matches what I see. The stair treads are broad horizontal bands of one sand tone, each with only a thin highlight and shadow line. The only grain is a few speckles along the lower band, and there are no per-step wear dots, no stone or grain clusters, and no scattered variation. Each band uses about 3-4 steps, where Beodeul materials use 5-6. As a result the stairs read as flat stripes, not a carved cliff cut with depth. A careful artist would find it flatter and more sticker-like than the references, so it fails.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a sand patch built from a few horizontal bands (light top, mid sand, then darker step lines) with only sparse speckle. Tone count is acceptable (6 visible tones per tile, against 3 for grass and 7 for paving), and the edge tint is warm brown rather than neutral (0% near-neutral), so the outline reads as dark material tone. It still falls short of the references in other ways. 21% near-flat coverage, where both references have 0%, shows large flat bands of one colour with no grain, scallop or per-step highlights. Only 7 raw colours are spread across about 4 real shading steps, against the roughly 6 per material that Beodeul uses. The step risers and treads read as flat stripes rather than a shaded cut through a cliff, and the surface does not have the grain or clumping of the grass or the stone-by-stone shading of the paving. At the same scale it looks flatter and more sticker-like than either reference.
